unitTitle: Mental and Emotional Health: Stress, Coping, and Help-Seeking
title: Application or project: recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management
focus: recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management
essentialQuestion: How do I manage stress in a way that still works on a bad week, and how do I ask for help early?
materials: a guardian-approved list of local and national help resources
keyPoints: When distress is persistent, worsening, unsafe, or interfering with sleep, school, relationships, or daily tasks, self-management should expand to trusted-adult or professional support.
A durable plan names the goal, constraints, feasible options, support and backup routes, plus the evidence or condition that should trigger review and revision.

For recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Build a two-tier support plan: strategies the learner can run alone, and the named point at which they contact a trusted adult or professional. The plan may be written entirely with general categories rather than personal detail.
studentTask: Build a decision organizer for a fictional person working on recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management. Record the goal, two influences or constraints, two options, the safest feasible choice, a support or backup route, and the evidence that would trigger a later revision.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the recognizing when a difficulty is bigger than self-management task using the supplied fictional or public case.
